ncsu_ext_phytophthora_blight_peppers.publisher: NC State Extension, NC State University Vegetable Pathology Lab
ncsu_ext_phytophthora_blight_peppers.citable_for: NC State vegetable pathology factsheet (Lina Quesada-Ocampo; published 29 June 2018, revised 9 Jan 2023) on Phytophthora capsici in pepper: pathogen and oospore survival (over 10 years), spread via water and splash, host range (peppers, eggplant, tomato, beans, most cucurbits; cereals are not hosts, so rotation is weak), symptoms (crown and fruit rot, wilting, girdling crown lesions, white cottony mold on fruit), favorable conditions (excessive rainfall or overhead irrigation, saturated soils, 75 to 90 F), and management (resistant varieties, good drainage and even terrain, raised beds and plastic mulch, moderate drip irrigation from a well, remove diseased plants and culls, rotate to cereals; home gardeners have no effective chemical option). umass_ext_itersonilia_canker.title: Carrot & Parsnip, Itersonilia Canker
umass_ext_itersonilia_canker.publisher: UMass Amherst Center for Agriculture, Food, and the Environment (Extension Vegetable Program)
umass_ext_itersonilia_canker.citable_for: UMass fact sheet (last updated 14 Jan 2013) on Itersonilia (black) canker of parsnip and carrot: cankers mainly on crown and shoulder; serious especially in late-harvested crops; favored by cool, wet weather; controls: resistant cultivars, rotate with non-host crops, control carrot rust fly, fungicide sprays not effective on root cankers, cover the shoulder of parsnips with soil throughout the growing season, deep plowing to decompose residue.
